alt: Two boxes. The alternative hypothesis predicts that participants who learn 20 words in silence will recall more words than those who learn while music plays. The null hypothesis predicts no difference in words recalled. The independent variable (silence or music) and the dependent variable (number of words recalled) are highlighted in both.
caption: The alternative predicts an effect, the null predicts none; both name measurable variables.

alt: The independent variable (silence versus music) is linked by an arrow to the dependent variable (number of words recalled). Extraneous variables such as time of day, noise outside and familiarity of the words can also affect the dependent variable; one that changes along with the IV becomes a confounding variable.
caption: Change the IV, measure the DV, and keep everything else from interfering.

alt: Three cards: a laboratory experiment has a controlled setting with the IV manipulated; a field experiment has a natural setting with the IV still manipulated; a natural experiment has an IV that varies naturally. A bar runs from more control to more true to life, and each card has a matching weakness.
caption: Moving from laboratory to natural experiments trades control for realism.

alt: Three rows. Independent groups: different participants in conditions A and B, controlled by random allocation. Repeated measures: the same participants in both conditions, controlled by counterbalancing. Matched pairs: matched participants split one per condition, using pre-testing to match. Each row gives a strength or weakness.
caption: Different people, the same people, or matched pairs: each design has its own control.

alt: Counterbalancing: half the participants do condition A then B and half do B then A, spreading practice and fatigue effects evenly. Random allocation: names drawn from a hat give each participant an equal chance of either condition so participant variables balance out. A note warns not to confuse random allocation with random sampling.
caption: Counterbalancing fixes order effects; random allocation balances participant variables.

alt: Four grids of people, each showing a different selection: random picks scattered across the population; opportunity picks a cluster of whoever is available; systematic picks every nth person; stratified picks from each subgroup in proportion. Each panel lists a strength and a weakness.
caption: Only random and stratified sampling aim for a representative sample; opportunity is quickest.

alt: Two proportion bars. The population of 600 is 360 girls (60%) and 240 boys (40%); the sample of 50 keeps the same proportions, 30 girls and 20 boys. Steps: girls are 360 ÷ 600 = 60%, 60% of 50 is 30, then choose each group at random.
caption: A stratified sample copies the population's proportions: 30 girls and 20 boys out of 50.
